title: Career Roadmap: Requirements Engineer
summary: A four-year undergraduate roadmap for learning how to capture stakeholder needs, translate them into clear and testable requirements, and help engineering teams deliver systems that solve the right problems.

blocks.text: arendi.ch
Recommended degree
B.Tech / B.E. in Systems Engineering
Target role
Requirements Engineer
Preparation timeline
4 years
Core focus
Requirements, systems thinking, verification

rows.text: Systems Requirements Engineer, Business Requirements Analyst, Systems Analyst, Requirements Analyst, Product Requirements Analyst
Requirements engineering, systems modelling, stakeholder analysis, verification and validation, technical documentation
Engineering organisations, software companies, aerospace, automotive, manufacturing, medical devices, infrastructure and technology consulting
Engineering degree plus requirements documentation, modelling, analytical and communication skills
M.Tech / M.S. in Systems Engineering, Systems Architecture, Industrial Engineering, Software Engineering or a related field

blocks.label: Important distinction
blocks.text: Requirements engineering is not simply writing documents. It involves discovering stakeholder needs, negotiating conflicting priorities, defining measurable system behaviour and maintaining traceability from requirements through design, testing and delivery. Some regulated or safety-critical sectors also require domain-specific standards and experience.

sections.heading: What does a Requirements Engineer do?

blocks.text: A Requirements Engineer connects stakeholders who need a system with the technical teams responsible for designing, building and testing it.
Typical responsibilities include:

blocks.label: Elicit requirements
blocks.text: Interview users, customers, engineers and business stakeholders to understand their needs.

blocks.label: Analyse stakeholder needs
blocks.text: Identify ambiguities, contradictions, missing requirements, dependencies and constraints.

blocks.label: Define system requirements
blocks.text: Convert broad needs into clear, measurable and verifiable statements.

blocks.label: Document specifications
blocks.text: Prepare stakeholder requirements, system requirements, use cases, interface requirements and acceptance criteria.

blocks.label: Model system behaviour
blocks.text: Use diagrams, workflows, use cases and system models to communicate complex behaviour.

blocks.label: Manage traceability
blocks.text: Link requirements to architecture, design components, test cases and validation evidence.

blocks.label: Control changes
blocks.text: Assess the impact of new requests on scope, cost, schedule, safety and existing interfaces.

blocks.label: Support verification and validation
blocks.text: Help teams determine whether the system meets its specifications and satisfies stakeholder needs.

blocks.label: Coordinate engineering teams
blocks.text: Work with software, hardware, testing, product, operations and quality teams.

blocks.label: Maintain compliance evidence
blocks.text: In relevant industries, support audits and standards-driven engineering documentation.
1. Systems Requirements Engineer
Defines requirements for complex systems containing software, hardware, people, processes and external interfaces.

blocks.label: Key skills
blocks.text: stakeholder analysis, system boundaries, interfaces, traceability and verification planning.
2. Business Requirements Analyst
Identifies business needs, maps current and proposed workflows, and converts objectives into requirements for technology or operational change.

blocks.label: Key skills
blocks.text: interviews, process modelling, user stories, acceptance criteria and stakeholder communication.
3. Automotive and Embedded Systems Requirements Engineer
Defines functional and performance requirements for vehicle electronics, embedded software and connected systems.

blocks.label: Key skills
blocks.text: system interfaces, embedded fundamentals, verification, safety and configuration management.
4. Aerospace and Safety-Critical Requirements Engineer
Specifies and traces requirements for complex systems where reliability, safety and formal evidence are essential.

blocks.label: Key skills
blocks.text: rigorous traceability, verification evidence, configuration control and relevant industry standards.
5. Software and Product Requirements Engineer
Translates product goals and user needs into software behaviour, functional specifications and testable acceptance criteria.

blocks.label: Key skills
blocks.text: requirements management, APIs, user stories, Agile workflows and test collaboration.

blocks.text: The objective is to graduate with strong engineering fundamentals, practical requirements-analysis skills, experience with systems modelling and a portfolio showing how requirements connect to design and testing.
Year 1 — Engineering and analytical foundations
Develop structured thinking, communication and technical literacy.
Academic subjects

items.text: Engineering mathematics and statistics
Introduction to systems and engineering design
Programming fundamentals with Python or C
Basic electronics and engineering physics
Technical communication and engineering drawing

blocks.text: Skills to develop

items.text: Structured problem-solving and logical reasoning
Writing precise, unambiguous technical statements
Flowcharts, process diagrams and basic UML concepts
Excel or spreadsheet-based analysis
Git, documentation organisation and version control basics

blocks.text: Practical projects

items.text: Document requirements for a student attendance system.
Create a workflow for a college laboratory booking process.
Develop a stakeholder map for a simple engineering project.
Prepare a problem statement, assumptions and constraints document.

blocks.label: Year-end outcome
blocks.text: Explain a problem clearly, identify stakeholders and produce a concise, organised engineering specification.
Year 2 — Requirements analysis and system modelling
Learn to discover, structure and validate system requirements.
Academic subjects

items.text: Systems engineering fundamentals
Object-oriented analysis and design
Database management and software engineering
Probability, reliability and quality fundamentals

blocks.text: Technical skills

items.text: Stakeholder interviews, workshops and observation
Functional versus non-functional requirements
Use cases, user stories and acceptance criteria
UML use-case, activity, sequence and state diagrams
Requirements prioritisation and conflict resolution
Basics of requirements traceability

blocks.text: Practical projects

items.text: Requirements specification for an online appointment system.
Use-case and activity diagrams for an industrial monitoring system.
Requirements traceability matrix connecting requirements to tests.
A review exercise identifying ambiguous or untestable statements.

blocks.label: Experience target
blocks.text: Join an engineering project team, contribute to documentation for a software project or seek a business-analysis internship.

blocks.label: Year-end outcome
blocks.text: Create a structured requirements document with diagrams, assumptions, acceptance criteria and a basic traceability matrix.
Year 3 — Systems architecture, verification and validation
Connect requirements to system design, interfaces and test evidence.
Academic subjects

items.text: System architecture and interface design
Verification, validation and testing
Reliability engineering and risk analysis
Project management and configuration management
Software or hardware integration, depending on specialisation

blocks.text: Technical skills

items.text: Requirements decomposition and allocation
Interface requirements and system boundaries
Requirements traceability across the engineering lifecycle
Change-impact analysis and version control
Acceptance testing, test planning and verification evidence
Model-based systems engineering (MBSE) fundamentals

blocks.text: Practical projects

items.text: Define system requirements for an automated greenhouse.
Develop a verification matrix with test methods and pass criteria.
Model interfaces between sensors, controllers and software.
Assess the impact of a requirement change on design and testing.

blocks.label: Experience target
blocks.text: Seek an internship in systems engineering, quality engineering, product analysis, embedded systems or technical documentation.

blocks.label: Year-end outcome
blocks.text: Demonstrate traceability from stakeholder needs to system requirements, design elements and verification tests.
Year 4 — Industry-aligned systems engineering
Demonstrate requirements ownership on a complete engineering project.
Academic and advanced topics

items.text: Advanced requirements management
Systems architecture and interface management
Risk, reliability and safety analysis
Engineering lifecycle and change control
Agile requirements and product lifecycle management
Domain-specific standards, where applicable

blocks.text: Practical projects

items.text: A full requirements baseline for a connected vehicle subsystem or industrial control system.
A complete requirements-to-test traceability matrix.
A change-request assessment with impact analysis.
A capstone with stakeholder needs, architecture, verification plans and review evidence.

blocks.text: Career preparation

items.text: Practise requirements-writing and ambiguity-detection exercises.
Prepare system-modelling and traceability examples.
Learn to explain trade-offs, assumptions and constraints.
Build a portfolio of redacted or original project artefacts.
Prepare for requirements, systems analysis and technical communication interviews.

blocks.label: Graduation outcome
blocks.text: Aim to have two or more substantial engineering case studies, one end-to-end requirements project, internship or team-project experience and a clear understanding of requirements through verification.

rows.text: Interviews, workshops, negotiation and conflict resolution
Use cases, activity diagrams, state models and architecture views
Requirement IDs, links, baselines and coverage
Test planning, acceptance criteria and evidence
Risk identification, failure analysis and reliability concepts
Impact analysis, versioning and configuration control
APIs, databases, software lifecycle and basic scripting

blocks.text: Essential requirements-writing principles
A good requirement should be:

blocks.label: Necessary
blocks.text: It addresses a genuine stakeholder or system need.

blocks.label: Clear
blocks.text: It has one intended interpretation.

blocks.label: Verifiable
blocks.text: A defined method can establish whether it has been met.

blocks.label: Feasible
blocks.text: It can be achieved within technical and operational constraints.

blocks.label: Traceable
blocks.text: Its source and downstream implementation or verification links are known.

blocks.label: Consistent
blocks.text: It does not contradict other approved requirements.
Example:
Weak requirement
“The system should be fast and user-friendly.”
Better requirement
“Under the specified test load of 500 concurrent users, the system shall return a successful search response within 2 seconds for at least 95% of valid search requests.”
The threshold and workload are illustrative. Real values should come from stakeholder needs, feasibility analysis and an agreed test environment.
Requirements management
IBM DOORS Next, Jama Connect, Siemens Polarion ALM or a suitable requirements repository
Systems modelling
SysML-capable modelling tools, UML tools and architecture-diagram applications
Project and backlog management
Jira, Azure DevOps, issue trackers and backlog-management tools
Documentation
Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint, structured templates and collaborative documentation tools
Process and diagrams
Draw.io, PlantUML, workflow diagrams and modelling software
Testing and verification
Test-management tools, test matrices, defect trackers and validation evidence repositories
Engineering collaboration
Git, version control, change requests, review workflows and configuration management

blocks.label: Tool-selection advice
blocks.text: Start with diagrams, spreadsheets, a version-controlled requirements repository and a traceability matrix. Learn a specialised requirements-management or MBSE tool when a project or target employer requires it. Many professional platforms are licensed, so check student editions and free alternatives before purchasing.

sections.heading: Portfolio projects that demonstrate requirements engineering

blocks.text: Your portfolio should show that you can turn an unclear problem into structured, testable and traceable requirements.
Project 1 — Requirements specification for a booking system
Beginner
Year 1–2

blocks.label: Build
blocks.text: Define requirements for a college laboratory, appointment or equipment-booking system.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: Stakeholder register, scope statement, functional and non-functional requirements, use cases and acceptance criteria.

blocks.label: Demonstrate
blocks.text: Clear writing, stakeholder analysis, prioritisation and ambiguity removal.
Project 2 — Requirements traceability and verification matrix
Intermediate
Year 2–3

blocks.label: Build
blocks.text: Define a system such as a smart irrigation controller and map stakeholder needs to system requirements and test cases.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: Requirement IDs, source links, verification method, acceptance criteria, status and coverage summary.

blocks.label: Demonstrate
blocks.text: Traceability, testability, requirement coverage and change management.
Project 3 — System architecture and interface requirements
Intermediate–Advanced
Year 3

blocks.label: Build
blocks.text: Specify an automated greenhouse or industrial monitoring system with sensors, a controller, a user interface and data storage.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: Context diagram, system decomposition, interface requirements, operational scenarios and verification plan.

blocks.label: Demonstrate
blocks.text: System boundaries, interface clarity, dependencies and allocation of requirements to components.
Project 4 — Change-impact analysis
Advanced
Year 3–4

blocks.label: Build
blocks.text: Simulate a change request—for example, increasing the number of connected devices or adding a security constraint—and analyse its consequences.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: Change request, affected-requirement list, dependency map, risk assessment, test updates and approval record.

blocks.label: Demonstrate
blocks.text: Impact analysis, engineering trade-offs, configuration control and decision documentation.
Project 5 — End-to-end systems engineering capstone
Advanced
Year 4

blocks.label: Build
blocks.text: Develop a complete requirements package for an original system, such as a smart energy monitor, autonomous delivery prototype or connected medical-device concept.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: Stakeholder needs, system requirements, architecture, interface specifications, risk register, traceability matrix and verification/validation plan.

blocks.label: Demonstrate
blocks.text: Requirements ownership across the lifecycle and the ability to connect business needs to engineering evidence.
What every portfolio project should contain

items.text: A problem statement, scope and list of stakeholders.
Explicit assumptions, constraints and out-of-scope items.
Unique requirement identifiers and a consistent naming convention.
Requirements written in clear, verifiable language.
Diagrams that communicate system behaviour and interfaces.
A traceability matrix linking requirements to design and tests.
A change log and examples of how feedback was incorporated.
A short explanation of trade-offs, unresolved risks and limitations.

blocks.text: Use original or appropriately anonymised project artefacts. Never publish confidential company requirements, customer information or restricted engineering documentation.
Suggested timeline

rows.text: Practise technical writing, process mapping and structured problem-solving.
Build requirements documents, diagrams and traceability matrices.
Apply for systems engineering, business analysis, quality engineering or product analysis internships.
Complete an end-to-end requirements capstone and apply for graduate requirements or systems engineering roles.

blocks.label: Application strategy
blocks.text: Include a sample requirements specification, a traceability matrix and a system diagram in your portfolio. Explain how you handled ambiguous requests, resolved conflicts and made requirements testable.
Focus on standards awareness, practical requirements analysis and systems modelling. Certifications can support your profile, but they do not replace engineering experience.

rows.text: Learn structured requirements engineering and explore CPRE certification
Understand systems engineering principles and professional pathways
Practise requirements, user stories, workflows and issue tracking
Study systems lifecycle, architecture and technical management
Understand software testing fundamentals relevant to requirements verification

blocks.text: Useful starting points:

items.text: IREB — Requirements Engineering
INCOSE — Systems Engineering

Atlassian — Agile resources

blocks.label: Potential certification route
blocks.text: explore the IREB Certified Professional for Requirements Engineering (CPRE) Foundation Level when your fundamentals are established. Check the current syllabus, exam rules, cost and prerequisites before registering. More advanced systems engineering credentials may have experience requirements.

Postgraduate study may help you specialise in systems architecture, complex engineering programmes, industrial engineering or safety-critical systems. It is not required for every entry-level Requirements Engineer position.

rows.text: Systems Requirements Engineer or Systems Architect

blocks.text: These are research starting points, not a claim that each institution offers a dedicated Requirements Engineering degree. Review current curricula, faculty expertise, admission criteria and the actual specialisation offered.
Progression depends on the complexity of systems handled, domain expertise, stakeholder ownership and the ability to lead requirements across the engineering lifecycle.

Possible long-term specialisations include:

blocks.label: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE)
blocks.text: Use system models to define and analyse architecture, behaviour and interfaces.

blocks.label: Safety and reliability
blocks.text: Work with hazard analysis, risk controls and verification evidence in relevant industries.

blocks.label: Software requirements
blocks.text: Focus on software behaviour, APIs, acceptance criteria and release requirements.

blocks.label: Systems architecture
blocks.text: Translate requirements into system structure, interfaces and technical decisions.

blocks.label: Requirements leadership
blocks.text: Manage baselines, stakeholder agreements, change control and traceability across large programmes.
Use this checklist to assess readiness for graduate Requirements Engineer, Systems Analyst and related positions.
Requirements Engineer readiness
Requirements fundamentals
Distinguish stakeholder needs, system requirements and design decisions
Write clear, unambiguous and verifiable requirements
Identify missing, conflicting and duplicate requirements
Analysis and modelling
Conduct a basic stakeholder interview or requirements workshop
Create use-case, activity or system-context diagrams
Define scope, assumptions, constraints and acceptance criteria
Traceability and verification
Build a traceability matrix linking requirements to tests
Explain verification versus validation with examples
Assess the impact of a requirement change
Tools and engineering lifecycle
Use a requirements repository or structured spreadsheet
Understand version control, baselines and change requests

blocks.label: Requirements quality
blocks.text: Rewrite vague statements into measurable, verifiable requirements.

blocks.label: Stakeholder analysis
blocks.text: Explain how you handle conflicting priorities and unclear requests.

blocks.label: Modelling
blocks.text: Draw a context diagram, use-case diagram or simple system architecture.

blocks.label: Traceability
blocks.text: Explain how you would connect a requirement to design and test evidence.

blocks.label: Change management
blocks.text: Assess what must be reviewed when a requirement changes.

blocks.label: Verification and validation
blocks.text: Distinguish whether a system meets its specification from whether it satisfies the actual stakeholder need.

blocks.label: Communication
blocks.text: Present technical trade-offs in language appropriate for both engineers and non-technical stakeholders.
Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE)

Learn to represent system structure, behaviour, interfaces and constraints through models. This is particularly useful for complex engineering projects where diagrams and structured models complement traditional documents.
AI-assisted requirements analysis
Explore tools that help identify ambiguity, duplicates, inconsistencies and missing test cases. Learn to validate suggestions manually and protect confidential project data.
Digital twins and connected systems
Understand how system requirements address real-time data, connectivity, interfaces, reliability, cybersecurity and integration between physical and digital components.
Verification automation and digital traceability
Develop skills in linking requirements to automated tests, maintaining evidence, tracking coverage and detecting changes across engineering artefacts.
Safety, cybersecurity and reliability requirements
Learn how to specify measurable constraints for security, resilience, fault handling, data protection and safe system behaviour. Domain-specific standards may apply in regulated sectors.

These skills can strengthen your profile as engineering systems become more connected and complex. AI tools can assist with analysis, but requirements still need stakeholder agreement, engineering judgement and appropriate verification.

Suggested final-year profile
By graduation, aim to demonstrate:

items.text: A strong understanding of requirements engineering principles.
The ability to write clear, testable and traceable requirements.
At least two detailed requirements-engineering case studies.
Experience with system diagrams and interface definitions.
A requirements traceability matrix linked to verification activities.
Familiarity with change control, versioning and review workflows.
Internship or team-project experience, where possible.
The ability to explain engineering decisions clearly to technical and non-technical stakeholders.

blocks.text: Requirements Engineer is a suitable career path for a student pursuing B.Tech / B.E. in Systems Engineering, especially if they enjoy analytical problem-solving, technical documentation, system architecture and collaboration across engineering teams.
The recommended route is to:

items.text: Build strong engineering fundamentals and systems thinking.
Learn stakeholder elicitation, requirements analysis and technical writing.
Practise UML or SysML modelling and requirements traceability.
Connect requirements to architecture, verification and validation.
Complete an end-to-end systems project and seek an industry internship.
Apply for roles such as Graduate Systems Engineer, Requirements Engineer, Systems Analyst or Business Analyst, depending on the job description.

blocks.text: The most important skill is the ability to translate a real stakeholder need into clear, feasible, verifiable and traceable engineering requirements. That capability is useful across software, automotive, aerospace, industrial automation and other complex engineering domains.
